questions.q: Which idea is von Neumann architecture built on?
options: Instructions and data are held together in the same main memory
Instructions are held in the CPU and data in memory
Each program gets its own separate processor
Data is held on secondary storage while a program runs
questions.feedback: The stored-program concept: one memory holding both the instructions and the data they work on.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 1: John von Neumann

questions.q: Give one reason the stored-program concept made computers much more useful.

markPoints.concept: the same machine can run a different program by loading different instructions
markPoints.exemplar: A different program can be loaded, so the same computer can do a different job.

questions.example: Loading a different set of instructions makes the same computer do a different job, instead of being rebuilt for each task.
questions.paraphrase: You can run new software on the same hardware rather than rewiring it.
questions.feedback: Before stored programs, changing the task meant changing the machine.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 1: John von Neumann

questions.q: In a von Neumann computer, instructions and data travel to the CPU along the same bus.
options: True
False
questions.feedback: True, and it is the architecture's main weakness: an instruction and the data it needs cannot be fetched at the same time.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 2: The stored-program concept

questions.q: Explain one disadvantage of storing instructions and data in the same memory, reached by the same bus.

markPoints.concept: only one of them can be fetched at a time
accept: one at a time|one by one|take turns|queue|share the bus|one after

not at the same time|cannot be fetched at the same time|cannot be read at the same time|not be fetched at the same time|cannot both|can not both|not simultaneous|not together|not at once|cannot be done at the same time|cannot happen at the same time
markPoints.exemplar: An instruction and its data cannot be fetched at the same time.

markPoints.concept: so the CPU may be left waiting, which slows the computer down
markPoints.exemplar: This means the CPU has to wait, so the program runs more slowly.

questions.example: Because both share one bus, an instruction and the data it needs cannot be fetched at the same time, so the CPU has to wait and the program runs more slowly.
questions.paraphrase: They have to take turns on the single bus, which leaves the processor idle and makes things slower.
questions.feedback: This is the von Neumann bottleneck. The second mark is for the consequence, not for naming it.
questions.hint: If two things need the same single road, what happens to the second?
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 2: The stored-program concept

questions.q: A program has just executed the instruction at address 42, and the next instruction is at 43. What does the program counter hold now?
options: The instruction itself
The result of the instruction
questions.feedback: The PC holds an address, not an instruction, and it was incremented during the fetch, so it already holds 43.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 3: Program counter and accumulator

markPoints.concept: the result of a calculation carried out by the ALU

questions.example: The result of the most recent calculation done by the ALU.
questions.paraphrase: Whatever the ALU just worked out.
questions.feedback: Results, not addresses. Addresses live in the PC and the MAR.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 3: Program counter and accumulator

questions.q: The CPU is about to write a value to address 100 in RAM. Which register holds the number 100?
options: The memory address register
The memory data register
The accumulator
The program counter
questions.feedback: The MAR holds the address, whether the CPU is reading or writing. The MDR holds the value itself.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 4: MAR and MDR

questions.q: Which statements about the MAR and MDR are true? Tick all that apply.
options: The MAR holds an address
The MDR holds data or an instruction
They are both inside the CPU
The MDR holds the address of the next instruction
The MAR holds the result of a calculation
correct: The MDR holds data or an instruction
They are both inside the CPU
questions.feedback: Address in the MAR, contents in the MDR, both of them registers inside the CPU. The address of the next instruction is the program counter's job.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 4: MAR and MDR

questions.q: How does Harvard architecture differ from von Neumann architecture?
options: It keeps instructions and data in separate memories with separate buses
It has no registers inside the CPU
It stores programs on secondary storage rather than in memory
It can only run one program at a time
questions.feedback: Separate memories and separate buses, which is why an instruction and data can be fetched at the same time.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 5: Other architectures

questions.q: A company is designing the controller for a washing machine and is choosing between von Neumann and Harvard architecture. Explain one reason Harvard architecture might be chosen.

markPoints.concept: instructions and data are in separate memories with separate buses
markPoints.exemplar: Harvard architecture has separate memories and buses for instructions and data.

markPoints.concept: so both can be fetched at the same time, which suits a device that must respond predictably
markPoints.exemplar: This means an instruction and its data can be fetched at the same time, so the controller responds faster.

questions.example: Harvard architecture uses separate memories and buses for instructions and data, so an instruction and the data it needs can be fetched at the same time, which makes the controller respond more quickly and more predictably.
questions.paraphrase: Because the program and the data are in different memories with their own buses, both can be read simultaneously, giving faster and more predictable response.
questions.feedback: Separate buses, therefore simultaneous fetches. The second mark needs the 'therefore'.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, station 5: Other architectures

questions.q: Sort each item into where it belongs.
questions.feedback: Everything with 'register' or 'unit' in its name here is inside the processor. RAM and the drive are not.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.1 Lesson 2 — Von Neumann HQ, Final challenge: name that part

questions.q: Which list puts these in order from fastest to slowest to access?
options: Register, cache, RAM, solid state drive
Cache, register, RAM, solid state drive
RAM, register, cache, solid state drive
Register, RAM, cache, solid state drive
questions.feedback: Speed runs the opposite way to size: the smallest store is the fastest.
